set.hook: A candlelit dining room inside a coral cave on the Diani shore, open to the sky since 1983.
set.why: George and Jackie Barbour opened the cave to diners in 1983 and named it with a pun: Ali Baba's cave, with the family name worked in. The coral is put at 120,000 to 180,000 years old. Only the kitchen and the washrooms were built; the rest is as the sea left it, ten metres below ground, with a hole to the sky and a sliding cover for rain nights. About seventy diners a night, split across two sittings.

set.hook: Almanara's beach pavilion of white canvas on steel, cooking what the resort's own boat brings in.
set.why: Sails is the restaurant of Almanara, a villa resort on Galu that has sold itself on 'bespoke experiences since 2007'. The roof is a run of white canvas canopies on a steel frame, cut to echo a dhow's sails. Fish comes from the resort's own boat and vegetables from its organic garden, and some of the catch is smoked in-house. Day visitors are welcome, so a single drink at sundown is a fair way to see it. Sources disagree on who now leads the kitchen.

set.hook: Sushi, wood-fired pizza and aged steaks off one beachfront menu, from breakfast until late evening.
set.why: Nomad is the beach restaurant of the resort long known as The Sands at Nomad, and one kitchen covers a lot of ground: hand-rolled sushi with mangrove crab, Roman-style pizza from a wood oven, a Swahili and Indian corner, and steaks aged in Laikipia. Produce comes from the group's own farm and from local fishermen. The June 2026 menu prints prices with VAT, catering levy and service already included, so the number you read is the number you pay.

set.hook: A Japanese-family sushi and teppanyaki room on the Diani strip, cutting sashimi from the local catch.
set.why: Shashin-Ka is run by a Japanese family with a Japanese chef, according to the Galu villa operator Aestus, which sends its own guests here. The menu is short and traditional: sashimi and nigiri cut from the reef fish and tuna landed along this coast, tempura, and teppanyaki at the grill. It appears in Potentash's Kenyan food guide and on the Ocean Tribe dive crew's list of where residents eat, and diners were still reviewing it in July 2026.

set.hook: A small beach hotel's open bistro on Diani sand, with sockets, wifi and an all-you-can-eat Friday barbecue.
set.why: Asha is a small boutique hotel directly on Diani beach, and its bistro serves outside diners from breakfast through dinner. In a 2022 survey of places to work along the strip, it was the only beachside room with proper laptop seating, enough sockets and usable wifi, measured at 30 Mbps down. The kitchen leans on Indian Ocean seafood and market produce, and Friday nights are an all-you-can-eat barbecue with a live guitarist.

set.hook: Ida and Filip Andersson's beach home at Kinondo, beside the kaya forest; dinner moves to a new spot nightly.
set.why: Kinondo Kwetu means 'our home at Kinondo'. It opened as a small hotel in 2005 on a private beach south of Galu, and Ida and Filip Andersson still live there and host in person. Their Kinondo Kwetu Trust founded the local health centre in 2008, which had logged more than 150,000 patient visits by 2023. Dinner is set somewhere different each evening, on the sand, among the trees or at a villa, from fresh seafood and garden vegetables.

set.hook: An adults-only beach hotel in north Diani whose kitchen keeps no fixed meal times for its guests.
set.why: The Maji made its name on one house rule: guests eat what they like, when they like, where they like on the property, whether under the Indian almond tree, in the gazebo facing the ocean or on the pool deck after dark. The menu crosses Swahili, Indian and Mediterranean cooking with fish from the day's boats, and dietary requests are routine. It has about fifteen rooms and was listed among Tripadvisor's 2026 Travellers' Choice hotels.

set.hook: A resort on a mangrove island off the Kwale shore, sharing its ground with a sacred Digo kaya grove.
set.why: Chale is a 31-acre island about 600 metres off the mainland, two-thirds mangrove and forest. Its southern end is sacred Digo kaya land and cannot be built on. The resort, renamed from The Sands at Chale Island after a 2024 renovation, runs several restaurants and an overwater bar for sundown. Since 2021 the island has also been the subject of a land-recovery case in which the anti-corruption commission argues it is a protected public monument.

set.hook: Galu's reef fishermen beach their boats here on the morning tide; buy whole fish and octopus off the sand.
set.why: Mwaepe is one of seven artisanal landing stations in the Diani-Chale reef fishery, which marine scientists have studied since the late 1990s, and it is the one within walking distance of the Galu hotels. The site lies inside the Diani-Chale Marine Reserve, managed by KWS. Its Beach Management Unit won the ground back from land-grabbers and now holds the title, and a KSh 256 million World Bank-funded rebuild, with an ice plant and boatyard, began in 2025.

The Coast (5 Aug 2026) reports KPA fish-preservation facilities across Msambweni landing sites but it is unclear how much applies to Mwaepe. No 2026-dated proof of daily trading found, so old date kept.

set.hook: Tuna and kingfish land at Shimoni village, beside a new state fish port still awaiting its operators.
set.why: The Shimoni channel is deeper water than Diani's reef, so the boats here bring in bigger fish: tuna and kingfish. Next to the village landing stands the state fish port, built by the Kenya Ports Authority with a jetty rated for 200 tonnes a day, a cold store and an ice plant. It was finished and handed over in 2025; the Deputy President inspected it in February 2026, and in March the government began bringing in private operators. The village landing remains the working market.

shimoni-landing.evidence: The Star, 28 Feb 2026: DP Kindiki inspects the Sh2.7bn port, described as complete and awaiting operationalisation. Mjengo Hub, 19 Mar 2026: government begins bringing in private operators. No source found confirming commercial landings at the port as of Oct 2026 (a Sep 2026 Kenya Times feature is unclear).

shimoni-landing.hot: Spring tides around 26 Oct and 24 Nov; the KPA fish port is still waiting for an operator (Feb 2026 report).

set.hook: Ukunda's covered market at Mvindeni, opened by the President in May 2026, with cold rooms behind the veg rows.
set.why: For years Ukunda's traders sold in the open, in dust and rain, with goods stolen overnight. The covered market at Mvindeni replaced that: more than two hundred stalls, eateries, cold storage for perishables, borehole water and floodlights. President Ruto opened it on 23 May 2026. By August the traders were saying business was picking up and asking for credit to grow, while some sellers still worked the roadside outside the gates.

diani-modern-market.hot: The first mangoes of the season arrive in November; the main crop runs December to March.

set.hook: A small Ukunda canteen cooking coast biryani with tangy chicken mchuzi and samosas fried fresh.
set.why: Moiz is a working lunch room rather than a place to linger. Coast-style biryani is the reason to come, served with a sharp chicken mchuzi spooned over the rice, alongside pilau and vegetable samosas made that day. Listings place it variously on Hospital Road, Diani Palm Road and in the Diani Legend Store building, all in the streets behind the beach road. Its live delivery listing is the best day-to-day sign that the kitchen is cooking.

set.hook: Ukunda's town grill opposite Equity Bank: charcoal chicken, whole fish and octopus soup, far from the beach.
set.why: Karafuu means clove in Swahili, and this is a town kitchen, opposite Equity Bank in Ukunda rather than on the beach strip. The fire handles chicken and mutton choma and whole fish, and the pot handles pweza, an octopus soup sold for KES 300 in August 2026. Pilau and chips masala round it out, and its own page also offers seafood pizza. A second branch, Golden Karafuu, sits at the north end of the beach road, and Glovo delivers across Diani.

set.hook: A makuti-roofed canteen between Ukunda and the beach road: pilau, biryani and fish for the neighbourhood.
set.why: Swahili Pot is a garden canteen under a makuti roof on the road between Ukunda town and Diani, and belongs to the same family as the long-running African Pot in Ukunda. The cooking is coastal home food: pilau first, then biryani, fried and grilled fish, and ukwaju, the sour tamarind juice. Most residents order it through Glovo on weeknights, and that live delivery listing is also how its trading is checked.

set.hook: A Sicilian family's wood-oven Italian on the beach road, with handmade pasta and gelato to their own recipe.
set.why: Mario Scianna, from Sicily, opened Leonardo's on the Diani strip more than twenty years ago, and his son Roberto has run it since around 2019. The pizza is Roman-style, slow-risen and baked in a wood oven; pasta is made by hand. The family says theirs was the first true Italian gelato made in Diani, using methods from Mario's home town. In March 2024 Jackson Biko of Business Daily compared the lit makuti dining room at night to an ocean liner.

set.hook: Aniello's long-running pizzeria near Leonardo's, with a wood oven and a pizza list that runs to about fifty.
set.why: Aniello, an Italian who settled on the south coast decades ago, has run this pizzeria as a family business for most of the strip's modern history. The oven is wood-fired and the menu leans Neapolitan, with simple fish plates alongside; the French guide Petit Fute counted some fifty pizzas on the list. Residents, the Ocean Tribe dive crew among them, keep naming it as their local Italian. Diners were still reviewing it in March 2026, though it publishes no website or hours.

set.hook: Diani's café of record since 2000: espresso, the house kokkoccino and bistro plates for the weekday crowd.
set.why: Kokkos opened in 2000, when the Diani strip had almost no serious coffee, and for years it was the one place to get it. The house drink is the kokkoccino, a flavoured cappuccino named after the café. The kitchen plates bistro food with local, Asian and European threads, and on weekdays the tables fill at lunch with residents, NGO staff and hotel managers. set.hook: A deaf-staffed café on Galu sand where you order coffee using the sign language printed on the menu.
set.why: Feisal Hussein founded Pallet in Nairobi in 2019 to train and employ deaf and hard-of-hearing waiters. That first café closed on 15 April 2026 to make room for a petrol station, which left the Galu beach branch, open since 2023, as the brand's centre. There are no walls: hammocks, beach beds and makuti umbrellas, plus a corner for laptops that doubles as a space for local art. Business Daily profiled Safari, a deaf staffer trained in-house on coffee and cocktails.

set.hook: A small artisan bakery beside Apero, baking German seed breads, challah and jam-filled Berliners.
set.why: Diani Bakehouse is locally owned and bakes bread that is hard to find on this coast: German seed loaves, challah, croissants, cinnamon rolls and Berliners filled with fruit preserves, with cakes and cupcakes to order. The German loaves are a trace of the European residents who built many of the strip's first hotels. Its own web page is a bare listing that places it next to Apero Bar and Restaurant, and it posts no opening hours at all.

set.hook: The Mwaepe fishing community's own family-run kitchen, frying the day's catch beside the landing beach.
set.why: This is the restaurant of the fishermen's village at Mwaepe, a few steps from Colobus Shade, and about as close as Diani gets to eating inside its fishery. Fish, prawns and calamari are fried or grilled to order above the beach where the ngalawa outrigger canoes come in. The village's Beach Management Unit took this land back from grabbers and holds its title, and a state-backed upgrade of the landing site began here in 2025.

set.hook: A sand-floored seafood kitchen at the Mwaepe landing, grilling lobster, crab and fish over charcoal.
set.why: Colobus Shade stands at Mwaepe, where Diani's reef fishermen land, and the charcoal grill works metres from where the boats come in. The order is the seafood platter of lobster, crab, prawns and fish, priced well below the beach-road restaurants: travellers reported a whole lobster at about KES 1,500 to 1,800 in 2023 and 2024. The owners are Muslim and serve no alcohol, so drink madafu instead. Residents and the Ocean Tribe dive shop send people here.

set.hook: Where Ukunda's matatu and boda crews eat after dark: viazi karai, mishkaki and roast maize at the crossroads.
set.why: The junction of the Diani beach road and the Likoni-Lunga Lunga highway is Ukunda's transport centre, and from late afternoon it turns into an open-air kitchen. Potatoes are dipped in turmeric batter and fried in karai pans as viazi karai, served with chilli and tamarind; mishkaki skewers go over the coals, and roast maize sells for about KES 20. The vendors have no names and change from night to night, so follow the queue of boda riders to the freshest oil.

set.hook: The Diani branch of Nairobi's Havana Bar, cooking from morning until 01:00 every day of the week.
set.why: Havana opened as the coast outpost of a long-running Nairobi bar, and its use is simple: the kitchen stays on until 01:00 every night. The menu runs from KES 70 mint water to a KES 4,000 seafood grill (August 2026), with pizzas, grilled calamari and Cuban-leaning plates in between. It sits by the road rather than on the beach, takes M-Pesa and delivers through Glovo, so it is where a crew finishing a late service can still eat.

set.hook: A courtyard cocktail bar opened in 2022 by the Salty Squid team, now a regular on regional award lists.
set.why: The team behind the Salty Squid opened Funky Monkey in July 2022 in a roadside courtyard. It became the first bar on the Kenyan coast listed on 50 Best Discovery, and the Tales of the Cocktail Spirited Awards named it in the Middle East and Africa top ten for Best International Bar Team and Best International Restaurant Bar in 2024, 2025 and 2026. The drinks fold Kenyan ingredients into classics: a smoked Negroni, a pineapple and basil smash.

set.hook: A beach bar in Diani's old Aga Khan Hall, built around a baobab by the pair who ran Nomad's bar.
set.why: When Forty Thieves, George Barbour's famous beach bar, closed after his death in 2018, Diani lost its meeting place. Claudia and Richard Glaser, who ran Nomad's beach bar for fourteen years, opened The 41 to fill that role, in what its own site calls the former Aga Khan Hall. The bar wraps an old baobab, the compound runs on solar, and there is a Koroga corner where you cook your own pot. Ocean Tribe's dive base works from the same site.

set.hook: The beach bar of the Kenyaways kite village at Galu, serving yellowfin and prawns as the kites come in.
set.why: The Salty Squid sits on the sand inside the Kenyaways kite village at Galu, next to the H2O Extreme kite school, which makes it the dining room of Diani's wind scene. Seared local yellowfin, garlic king prawns, dorado and reef lobster lead the menu, and the bar claims the largest gin list on the Kenyan coast. Oli and Hal, who run it, also opened Funky Monkey. set.hook: Wasini Island's original restaurant, serving dugout-landed crab since 1978 on the Kisite dhow day.
set.why: Charlie Claw's says it has fed visitors on Wasini since 1978. Crab and fish come ashore by dugout canoe and are eaten in an open room under palm thatch above the channel, and it holds the only bar licence on this mostly Muslim island. Its own jahazi dhows sail to Kisite under a twelve-point dolphin code: approach parallel, stay twenty minutes at most, never swim with or feed them. Its community fund pays teachers on both sides of the channel.

set.hook: A budget lodge and campsite on Tiwi beach whose palm-shaded bar is the stretch's only public kitchen.
set.why: Tiwi, north of Diani, has almost no restaurants: villas cook for themselves and fishermen sell straight off the sand. Twiga Lodge, a budget beachfront lodge and campsite, is the exception, with a bar and kitchen under the palms serving simple plates and cold beer. Camping ran at around KES 400 a head in 2025 listings. Reef walks described in 2026 still begin and end here, but other recent reports are mixed, so arrive expecting drinks and be glad of food.

set.hook: Roaming coconut sellers on Diani and Galu sand: green nuts opened by panga, then split for the jelly.
set.why: No one owns this trade; it walks the beach. Vendors carry green drinking coconuts and open them to order with a panga, and the settled price in 2026 was KES 50 to 100, with higher opening bids outside the big hotels. Drink the water, hand the nut back and ask for kuna: the vendor splits the shell, cuts a scoop from the husk, and you eat the soft young flesh inside.

set.hook: Before dawn, Ukunda's mama stalls fry cardamom-coconut mahamri for chai and pigeon peas; gone by eight.
set.why: Mahamri are triangles of dough flavoured with coconut and cardamom, fried before dawn by women working small pans along Ukunda's back streets and near the matatu stage. They sell for KES 30 to 50 each and are eaten with mbaazi ya nazi, pigeon peas in coconut, and spiced chai. The first batches are gone before 08:00, and the same benches cook biryani and pilau by late morning. There is no seated version worth naming: go early and point.

set.hook: Unsigned palm-wine rooms in Ukunda and the villages, pouring mnazi tapped that morning; go introduced.
set.why: Mnazi, the coconut palm wine of the coast, is drunk in mangwe, unmarked rooms in the back streets where selling has traditionally been women's work. Around 2,800 tappers work the coast. The drink was once criminalised; Kwale now licenses it, and in March 2024 the county ordered its roughly 4,000 sellers to reapply. A February 2026 Standard report found mnazi moving into modern lounges, supplied from Kwale and Kilifi groves. An outsider's verified way in is the Kaaribu tour's tasting stop.

set.hook: The kite school Boris Polo started as a Diani surf shack in 2003, now teaching on the flat Galu lagoon.
set.why: Boris Polo, born and raised in Kenya, opened H2O in 2003 as a surf shack on central Diani, then moved south to Galu because the mid-beach tides and boat traffic made teaching unsafe. That move is the whole argument for the place: on Galu the reef holds a wide, waist-deep lagoon flat at most states of tide. The IKO register lists its 2026 windows as 15 June to 14 September and 20 December to 20 March.

set.hook: Diani's oldest dive shop, running since 1985 from The Sands at Nomad, with its own artificial-reef wreck.

set.hook: Big-game charters out to the Pemba Channel drop-offs, releasing every billfish they hook.
set.why: Off Diani the continental shelf falls away fast into the Pemba Channel, so marlin water is a short run from the beach rather than half a day out. The club's boats, Princess Layla, Shuwari and White Dove, work those drop-offs and the Shimoni banks for blue, black and striped marlin, sailfish, wahoo and dorado. Billfish go back under a tag-and-release rule. In December 2024 its feed reported a Kenya-record 785 lb blue marlin.

Coral Spirit takes small groups upstream in traditional dugouts at the end of the day, paddling through the mangroves while herons and kingfishers settle, then back to the beach for drinks. It also runs paddleboarding on the same flat water and a beach bonfire barbecue as an add-on.

set.hook: A ninety-minute walk through Ukunda's market lanes and street kitchens, ending with palm wine.

set.hook: A sacred Digo forest you may enter only wrapped in a black kaniki cloth and led by a village guide.
set.why: Kaya Kinondo was closed to outsiders until 2001, when the Digo elders offered a sacrifice to the ancestors and opened it to guided visits: Kenya's first kaya ecotourism project. You remove any hat, tie on a black kaniki and promise not to kiss inside. The guide names medicinal trees, among them a 'pimple tree' used for acne, and stops short of the main shrine, which only elders may enter. Proceeds go to the village, schools and the forest.

set.hook: The Diani charity behind the rope 'colobridges' over Beach Road, with a rescue centre you can walk round.
set.why: Diani Beach Road was cut through coral-rag forest in 1971, and the Angolan colobus that live on either side kept trying to cross it. Colobus Conservation started in 1997 in response and began stringing rope bridges over the tarmac; it now counts more than forty across the region, and surveys from 2004 to 2020 credit them with a 70 percent rise in safe crossings. Vehicles still injure or kill around 55 primates a year on the strip.

set.hook: A no-take marine park of coral islets off Shimoni, where bottlenose, humpback and spinner dolphins feed.
set.why: Kisite-Mpunguti was gazetted in 1978 and covers 39 square kilometres of coral islets eleven kilometres off Shimoni, against the Tanzanian border. Three dolphin species use it: Indo-Pacific bottlenose on the reefs year-round, humpback dolphins in the channels, and spinners in pods of fifty to two hundred. From July to October humpback whales pass on their way north from Antarctic waters, and researchers have tracked them here since 2011. Single-use plastics are banned inside.

set.hook: A raised wooden walkway over fossil coral and mangrove at the edge of Wasini village, run by its women.
set.why: At high tide the sea pushes in under the planks and floods the dead coral heads, so the same walk looks completely different depending on when the dhow lands. KWS staff and villagers built the boardwalk with Kenyan and European biodiversity money, and the Wasini Women Group, around seventy members, runs it and keeps the fees for village welfare. The group's enterprise goes back to 1978. A small curio shop sits at the exit.

set.hook: A misty coastal rainforest reserve inland of Diani, home to Kenya's only sable antelope and a 25 m waterfall.
set.why: Shimba Hills was first protected as forest in 1903 and gazetted as a reserve in 1968; at 192.5 square kilometres it is the largest block of coastal rainforest left in Kenya. KWS describes its sable as the country's last breeding herd, best seen early around Giriama Point as they move down to drink. The ranger-escorted path to Sheldrick Falls takes up to an hour each way and ends at a drop of about 25 metres.

set.hook: The Gazi Bay village project that pays for wells and schoolbooks by selling mangrove carbon credits.
set.why: Mikoko pamoja means 'mangroves together'. The village at Gazi Bay protects 117 hectares of mangrove and replants several thousand trees a year, and was the first community anywhere to fund that work by selling blue-carbon credits. The money has gone into wells, school supplies and repairs. In July 2026 a German state secretary's delegation went out on the bay to see the plots. Visits mean an hour with the project team among the replanted rows.

set.hook: A volunteer turtle patrol that moves threatened nests to hotel hatcheries and calls releases at short notice.
set.why: Diani Turtle Watch started in 2012 as an offshoot of Local Ocean Trust in Watamu. Its monitors walk the beach each morning looking for tracks, move nests at risk from tides or people into hatcheries on hotel frontages, and wait 55 to 75 days for them to hatch. They also answer stranding calls and do post-mortems, which keep turning up plastic. One hotel hatchery alone reported nearly 1,300 hatchlings in its second season.

set.hook: A small roadside gallery of Kenyan painting near the GPS petrol station, with a portraitist on site.
set.why: Jimmy, the resident portrait painter, works from the gallery and takes commissions, so you can sit for a likeness or leave a photo and collect the canvas later in the trip. The walls run from large abstracts by Kenyan painters to Maasai beadwork and handcraft. It keeps published hours, including Sundays from September to February, which is unusual on this road, and it books safaris on the side.

set.hook: A Carrefour Market at Centre Point, Ukunda junction: fish counter, butchery, bakery and cold stores.
set.why: Majid Al Futtaim opened Kwale County's first Carrefour at Diani Centre Point Plaza in February 2021, a Carrefour Market format with 1,000 square metres of selling floor in its first phase. For a galley the useful parts are the chilled ones: a fresh fish counter, butchery, dairy and bakery, plus dry stores. Kentaste's coconut milk and cream, made a short drive inland, sit on its shelves.

set.hook: Chandarana's mid-strip branch at Baharini Plaza: spices, ghee, atta, wine and imported lines.
set.why: Chandarana is a Kenyan family chain, and its Diani branch at Baharini Plaza carries what the coast's own kitchens use: whole spices and masalas, ghee, atta and lentils from the Indian-Kenyan pantry, alongside imported goods, wine and spirits, fresh meat and produce. If a recipe calls for cardamom pods by the hundred gram rather than a jar, this is where to find them on the strip.

set.hook: Naivas at The Gate Mall in Ukunda, the supermarket where residents shop at town prices.
set.why: Naivas opened in Ukunda's Gate Mall in November 2015, taking a unit first booked for the now-failed Uchumi chain. Kenya's largest homegrown supermarket group prices for residents rather than beach visitors, and the store has a bakery, butchery and liquor section. It sits on the inland side of the junction, so it fits naturally into a run that starts at the Ukunda produce market.

set.hook: The coconut processor behind Kenya's supermarket coconut milk, with a factory at Kwale.
set.why: Kentaste was set up to give coast smallholders a steady price for nuts that mostly fell unused under millions of palms. It now buys from about 2,700 to 3,500 farmers, most of them certified organic and Fair for Life, and turns their coconuts into milk, cream, virgin oil, flour, desiccated coconut and baked coconut chips, which won New Product of the Year at the 2023 Africa Food Awards. Its factories are at Kwale and Malindi.

set.hook: Kenya's largest woodcarving co-operative, in Mombasa's Changamwe: open sheds where carvers work by hand.
set.why: This is a workplace, not a shop with a workshop attached: the sheds are open, the noise is real, and nobody stops working because you walked in. The co-operative sits in industrial Changamwe, off the Port Reitz road toward the airport, which is why the sensible way to see it is on the way to a flight. The store prices are fixed and fair, and a piece carries the carver's name if you ask.

set.hook: Mombasa's wholesale kanga and kikoi street, where tailors hem your cloth while you wait.
set.why: Nearly every kikoi and kanga sold on Diani's beach stalls is a factory print bought by the bale here, on Biashara Street in Mombasa's old commercial core. Mali ya Abdulla, the house of Kaderdina Hajee Essak, has traded on this street since 1907, and its name turns up printed into kanga borders. Each kanga carries a Swahili proverb along its edge, which is why buyers read the cloth before they look at the colour.

set.hook: A makuti-roofed bar and disco on Diani Beach Road, now selling itself as Manyatta Resort & Disco Lounge.
set.why: Manyatta's pull is that it fills early: one Business Daily reviewer found it busy by 20:30 on a weekend, on a strip where clubs usually start after eleven. It is an open-plan makuti bar with DJs, nyama choma and a mostly Kenyan crowd, and buying spirits by the bottle works out cheaper for a group. The place has rebranded as Manyatta Resort & Disco Lounge, adding rooms from KSh 4,000 and a rooftop lounge.
